Lenses In Triangle

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Roll a big circle along the base of a triangle and watch the lens it makes inside.
How to play: Drag the dot on the base, or focus it and use the left and right arrow keys. You can also use the slider, the − and + buttons, and the two checkboxes.
Look for the math

A circle as wide as the triangle is tall rolls along the bottom side. It always cuts the two sloping sides, and the small arc between those cuts keeps exactly the same size. The page asks us to prove that, and to check that the lens made from the arc stays in the triangle.

The arc never changes

Put the top corner at (0, 0), let the side be s, and put the circle's centre at (x, 0). Its radius is the triangle's height, h = √3 s / 2. Solving for where the circle meets the two sides gives points whose dot product from the centre does not depend on x. The angle at the centre is therefore always 60°, whatever the value of x. The test checks all 101 whole steps from −50 to 50 and finds no exception.

Why sixty degrees

Reflect C in A to get B' and reflect B in A to get C'. The line through A parallel to BC cuts the circle into equal halves. The two arcs inside the old and the reflected triangle are the same size. The angle BAC made by the lines BC' and B'C is an intersecting-chords angle: it is half the sum of those two equal arcs, so each arc is just 60°. Tick Hint to see the reflected triangle.

Where the lens sits

The chord DE leans by at most 30° when the circle is at either end of its roll, and by less than that in between. The reflected arc then cannot cross the sloping sides, so the lens stays inside. That is true while the circle rolls between the two ends that pass through B or C. The old Java scrollbar went five steps further, to 55: there the claim fails and the lens crosses AC. This port keeps the whole range and says so in the status line. Such a shape, which can turn while touching all sides, is a simple cousin of constant width.

Slide the roll to an end, tick Names, and watch D land exactly on B (or E on C). Then step past 50 and see the lens break out.
